title: CNI projects new U.S. tariffs could affect over a third of Brazilian exports
text:
CNI projects new U.S. tariffs could affect over a third of Brazilian exports
A projection by the National Confederation of Industry (CNI) shows that if new tariffs proposed by the United States Trade Representative (USTR) take effect, 31.6% of Brazilian exports to the U.S. would face a 37.5% tariff, representing an increase of 27.5 percentage points compared to the current rate of 10%, according to a June 15 report.
An additional 3.6% of exports would see tariffs rise from 10% to 12.5%, an increase of 2.5 percentage points. If these recommendations are implemented, a total of 35.2% of Brazilian exports to the United States would be subject to new tariffs.
Taking into account sectoral measures already in place under Section 232, up to 54.1% of Brazilian exports could be subject to some form of additional taxation, according to CNI's analysis.
The proposed measures do not have immediate effect and still require public consultation and hearings before any final decision is made by U.S. authorities.
Ricardo Alban, president of CNI, said, "A eventual imposição de novas tarifas não beneficia nenhum dos lados. Elas aumentariam custos para empresas, reduziriam a competitividade e criariam incertezas para investimentos. O caminho mais eficiente é o diálogo, baseado em critérios técnicos e na busca de soluções que preservem uma parceria econômica estratégica para ambos os países.”
Products such as pig iron are among those that would face an increased tariff from the current rate under Section 122 (10%) up to a potential total tariff burden of 37.5%. In 2024 alone, pig iron accounted for $1.5 billion in Brazilian exports destined for the United States.
The assessment takes into consideration exception lists published by USTR and maintains exemptions for products already covered under Section 232 measures as detailed in reports released by the agency.
In June this year, USTR released findings from two investigations conducted under Section 301 which directly impact Brazil: one focused on digital trade practices and related areas resulting in a proposed additional tariff of up to 25%, with exceptions for items such as coffee, orange juice and meat; another regarding forced labor practices across nearly ninety countries concluded with Brazil being included among nations not effectively restricting imports produced with forced labor—a situation prompting proposals for an extra tariff rate of up to 12.5%, again with certain exemptions.
When both measures apply simultaneously on specific products, cumulative additional tariffs may reach as high as 37.5%. The process will proceed through public consultations and hearings before any final determination is made by the U.S. government; public hearings are scheduled for July 6 and 7, at which companies and organizations can provide input or submit written statements.
